plan: Hello and work check (slide 1)

Same answer, same box (slide 9)
4 × 9 and 6 × 6 are both 36: the answer alone does not tell you the fact.
Multiply or add? (slides 10–13)

3.do: Read each fact aloud (or point to it on screen). She says the trick first, then the answer. Keep an "again" list and repeat those at the end.

5.do: Click one step at a time. She counts the jumps out loud on her fingers.
5.say: When a number is hiding, count how many 4s it takes to reach 24.
5.ask: Where do we land? How many jumps did it take?

8.do: She says her answer out loud; you tap it in. She can count jumps on her fingers.
8.listen: 8, 3, 9. If she says 28 or 12, she subtracted: ask, "Does 4 × 28 make 32?"

10.do: Read both stories aloud. She points out the word that tells you (each / every) or says it is missing.
10.say: Same numbers. Different job. The words decide, not the numbers.
10.ask: Which story has the clue word each?
10.listen: "Story A has each, so multiply: 24. Story B is just two piles, so add: 10."

11.do: Before answering she says the clue word (each or every) or says it is missing. She says the answer; you type it.

12.do: She tells you how many groups and how many in each; you set the buttons.

13.do: Click one step at a time. She says what we know and what the question asks before you click.
13.ask: Is 28 the answer? What does the question ask for?
13.listen: "No, 28 is all the stickers. It asks how many pages: 7."

2.title: Which plan worked better?
2.text: Think about How to Train Your Dragon.
prompts: What happened in the part you read since our last lesson?
Think of two different plans or ways characters tried to solve a problem. Which one worked better? Why?
Hiccup does not have big muscles. What does he have instead that helps him most? Give a reason from the book.
starters: Hiccup's best tool is … For example, …

notes.do: 4–5 minutes. She retells what happened in the part she read since Thursday, then evaluates two plans the characters tried.
notes.ask: "Think of two different plans characters tried. Which worked better? Why?"
notes.listen: A clear choice with a reason from the book.

6.do: Point to each tool on screen. Then read 6–9 facts aloud; she names the tool first, then the answer.
6.say: "Look at the factors first. Find the hard one. Then pick its tool."
6.listen: ×9: ×10 take away one group. ×6: ×5 plus one group. ×8: double three times. ×7: ×5 plus ×2.

7.do: She says the tool out loud, then the product; you type it. Time it for fun: all four in under a minute?
7.ask: "Which one took you the longest? Which tool would make it faster?"

9.do: Click through the steps. Point to the triangle: 7, 8 and 56. Keep it a preview: division is Week 4.
9.say: "Three numbers, four facts. Division undoes multiplication."

13.do: She says "equal groups or not?" out loud for every story, then says the operation; you type it. Then she solves it out loud.
13.ask: "What words in the story told you?"
13.listen: "each" or "every" for multiply; two different amounts for add.

14.do: You name a fact; she picks a tool and argues for it out loud.
14.say: "There can be more than one good path. I want your reason."
14.listen: Any correct path with a reason.
